# The Thrennel of Veshka

## The World

Veshka orbits a dim red dwarf so closely that it is tidally locked. One hemisphere bakes in endless daylight, and the other freezes in permanent night. Between them lies the **Twilight Belt**, a ring of perpetual dusk a few hundred kilometers wide. A ceaseless river of wind pours from the hot side toward the cold side, carrying dust, moisture, and drifting microorganisms. The Thrennel has built its entire existence around this wind.

## Appearance

An adult Thrennel looks like a tattered black sail anchored to the ground. Its body has three main parts:

- **The Root-Foot:** A dense, muscular base that drills up to two meters into the rocky soil. Once an adult anchors, it never moves again.
- **The Mast:** A flexible central stalk, four to six meters tall, made of hollow, cartilage-like rings. It bends nearly flat in storms and springs back upright when they pass.
- **The Veil:** A vast membrane, up to fifteen meters across, stretched between dozens of slender ribs that branch from the mast. It is velvety black, because on a world lit by a red sun, black absorbs the most energy. Up close, the Veil shimmers with faint violet iridescence from microscopic ridges that channel airflow.

Along the leading edge of the Veil runs a fringe of sticky filaments, the **combs**, which trail in the wind like the tentacles of a jellyfish.

## Feeding

The Thrennel is a filter feeder of the air. The wind from the dayside carries clouds of "drift," tiny airborne organisms, spores, and organic dust. The combs snag this material, and ripples of muscle along the ribs slowly pass it inward to digestive pores along the mast.

The Veil also does light work. Symbiotic microbes living in its tissue photosynthesize using the infrared-heavy light of the dim sun, which supplements the creature's diet. A well-fed Thrennel is warm to the touch even in the chilly twilight air.

## The Song

The most striking thing about the Thrennel is its sound. Wind passing through the hollow rings of the mast produces low, organ-like tones. The creature can tighten or relax muscles around each ring, changing the pitch, so it effectively plays itself like an instrument.

Thrennel forests stretch across the Twilight Belt in long rows perpendicular to the wind, and their songs carry for kilometers. Researchers believe the songs serve several purposes:

- **Warning:** A sudden shift to a sharp, dissonant chord ripples down the line when a predator approaches.
- **Coordination:** Before large dust storms, neighboring Thrennels harmonize and fold their Veils in unison.
- **Courtship:** During the breeding season, the songs become complex and layered, and individuals seem to "answer" one another.

## Life Cycle

A Thrennel does not begin life rooted in place. Juveniles, called **skitters**, hatch from seed-like pods as small, six-legged walkers about the size of a house cat. Their Veils are tiny and folded on their backs like beetle wings.

Skitters wander the Twilight Belt for several years, eating drift that settles on the ground and gliding short distances on their half-grown Veils. They are drawn to the songs of adult forests but never settle too close. Each skitter seems to look for a gap in the chorus, a place where its future voice won't be drowned out.

When it finds the right spot, the skitter drills its foot into the ground, and over the following months its legs are reabsorbed. Its mast lengthens and its Veil unfurls. From then on it is fixed in place and may live for several centuries.

To reproduce, adults release clouds of pollen-like spores into the wind, which carries them to Thrennels downwind toward the night side. Fertilized pods ripen at the base of the mast and burst open after several years, releasing a new generation of skitters.

## Predators and Threats

The Thrennel's main predator is the **gullet-moth**, a broad-winged flier that rides the same winds and chews holes in Veils to reach the nutrient-rich ribs. A damaged Veil can heal, but slowly, and a badly torn Thrennel may starve.

The greater danger is drift-starvation. When volcanic activity on the dayside shifts the wind patterns, entire forests can find their food supply cut off. Fossil records show long lines of ancient Thrennel root-foots, stone rings marking forests that fell silent when the wind changed.

## A Strange Detail

When a Thrennel dies, its Veil decays quickly, but its hollow mast hardens into a mineralized spire that can stand for thousands of years. The wind still blows through it and produces a single steady note that never changes.

Skitters avoid settling near these spires, and nobody knows why. One poetic theory holds that the young can tell the difference between a living voice and an echo, and won't build their lives among the dead. The Twilight Belt is dotted with these lonely, humming pillars, which travelers have named **the Remembering Stones**.

# The Sough of Verath

## The World
Verath is a tidally locked planet orbiting a dim red dwarf. One hemisphere bakes in permanent daylight, and the other lies frozen in endless night. Between them runs the Terminator, a ring of perpetual twilight a few hundred kilometers wide. Because hot air constantly rises on the dayside and rushes toward the cold nightside, the Terminator is swept by a wind that never stops. It has blown in the same direction for millions of years.

This wind carries life: clouds of microscopic spores, drifting algae, and tiny winged organisms that early researchers called *aeroplankton*. Feeding on that endless river of air is the creature colonists named the **Sough**, after the sound it makes.

## Anatomy
A Sough looks something like a cross between a kelp stalk, a ship's sail, and a pipe organ. Its body has three parts.

**The Anchor.** At its base is a muscular, many-lobed foot about the size of a cartwheel, ringed with hooked claws of a keratin-like material. The anchor clamps onto bare rock with enormous force. Prying a mature Sough loose takes heavy machinery. Inside the anchor lies the creature's nervous system: not a brain but a ring of interconnected ganglia, like a nerve net braided into a crown.

**The Stalk.** Rising from the anchor is a hollow, flexible column up to twelve meters tall, built from overlapping cartilage rings that let it telescope, bend, and twist. The stalk is lined with valves and vents the creature can open and close. Along its length run spiral rows of pit-eyes, tiny cups sensitive to infrared light. These let it "see" the warm bodies of predators and the glow of its neighbors.

**The Veil.** At the top unfurls the Sough's most striking feature: a translucent membrane sail up to twenty square meters, stretched across a lattice of fine, branching ribs. The veil is purple-black, a pigment evolved to absorb the red dwarf's deep-red and infrared light, and it photosynthesizes weakly. Its main job is filtration, though. Millions of sticky microscopic hairs coat its surface and catch aeroplankton from the wind, and waves of contraction ripple food down channels in the ribs to the stalk's interior, where it is digested.

## Behavior

**Singing.** Wind passing through the hollow stalk produces a low, breathy tone, and by adjusting its vents a Sough can shape that tone into a range of notes. Soughs grow in colonies of hundreds along ridgelines, and together they produce shifting chords that carry for kilometers. The first human survey team mistook the sound for a malfunction in their equipment.

Researchers now believe the songs are communication. Colonies change their harmonies when a predator approaches, when a solar flare is coming, and, most strangely, when a member of the colony dies. A gap in the chord persists for weeks, as if the others are leaving a space for the missing voice.

**Walking.** Soughs are not plants. During rare lulls in the wind, they move. A Sough releases half its anchor, swings its stalk forward, re-grips, and pulls the rest of its body after it, crawling like an inchworm at a few meters per day. They always travel upwind, toward the denser plankton clouds near the dayside edge, and they retreat when it grows too hot.

**Furling.** When the red dwarf flares and floods the surface with ultraviolet radiation, a colony's song shifts to a sharp, rising tone. Within minutes every Sough rolls its veil tight and retracts it into the top of the stalk like an umbrella pulled into its sheath. The ridgeline goes silent until the storm passes.

## Reproduction: The Long Return
The Sough's life cycle is its most remarkable trait. Once every few decades, a mature Sough releases thousands of seed-like larvae into the wind. They drift toward the nightside, where they land on the vast ice sheets and freeze solid, dormant but alive.

The ice of Verath's dark hemisphere is not still. Snow accumulates there endlessly, and the weight pushes glaciers slowly outward, back toward the Terminator. Over centuries the frozen larvae are carried in the ice like passengers on a conveyor belt until the glacier's edge melts in the twilight and releases them, sometimes five hundred years after their parent let them go.

The young Soughs that emerge crawl to the nearest rock, anchor, and begin to grow. Some colonies appear to recognize them. Newcomers are sometimes welcomed into a ridgeline with a burst of new harmonies, and genetic testing has shown that some newly thawed larvae settled within a few kilometers of colonies descended from their own ancestors.

## Ecology
Soughs are a keystone species. Their anchors break down rock into the first soils of the Terminator, small six-legged creatures called *pellucids* live in the folds of their veils and eat parasites, and their only serious predator, a low, armored climber called the *rasp*, has evolved to sneak up during flares, when the colonies are furled and blind.

A healthy Sough can live for three hundred years. The oldest known colony, on a ridge the survey team named the Choir, has been singing continuously for longer than human civilization has existed.

# The Veilstrider of Ossan-Tal

## The World

Ossan-Tal orbits a dim red dwarf and is tidally locked, so one face endures permanent day and the other permanent night. Between them runs the **Gloaming**, a ring of eternal twilight a few hundred kilometers wide. Here the sun hangs fat and crimson on the horizon, never rising or setting. Ossan-Tal's orbit is slightly eccentric, so the sun appears to rock back and forth across the sky over a 41-day cycle, and the band of habitable twilight drifts with it. Life in the Gloaming must either tolerate extremes or keep moving.

The Veilstrider keeps moving.

## Appearance

An adult Veilstrider stands about six meters tall but weighs only as much as a large dog. Its body is a translucent, teardrop-shaped bladder roughly the size of a hot-air balloon basket, suspended high above the ground on **five impossibly thin legs**. Each leg is jointed in four places and ends in a splayed, webbed "hand" that spreads its weight across the soft salt-crust flats.

The bladder is filled with a clear, gel-like fluid, and the creature is essentially a **living lens**. The dim red sunlight enters the curved upper surface and is focused onto a dense cluster of symbiotic organisms floating at its center, a glowing knot of dark violet filaments called the *heartweed*. These symbionts photosynthesize using infrared and deep-red light, invisible to human eyes, and share their sugars with their host. Seen from the side, a Veilstrider looks like a floating droplet of water with a bruise-colored ember burning inside it.

Draped from the underside of the bladder hangs the **veil**: hundreds of fine, ribbon-like tendrils up to three meters long that sway in the wind. They give the creature its name and serve several purposes at once.

## Senses

Veilstriders have no eyes in any familiar sense. Instead, the outer membrane of the bladder is dotted with thousands of tiny pigment spots that detect light direction. Because the whole body is a lens, the creature effectively "sees" by sensing where the focused sunlight lands on its inner surface. If the bright spot drifts off-center, the Veilstrider knows the sun has shifted and adjusts its heading.

The veil tendrils are exquisitely sensitive to vibration and chemistry. They taste the air, the brine pools beneath, and one another. Two Veilstriders meeting will drift close and let their veils intertwine, exchanging chemical signals in a slow, silent conversation that can last for hours.

## Feeding

Light alone isn't enough to sustain such a large creature, so the Veilstrider supplements its diet by wading. As it walks through the shallow brine lakes of the Gloaming, it lowers its veil into the water, where tiny sticky cells capture drifting plankton-like organisms and mineral-rich particles. The tendrils then curl upward and press their catch into small pores on the bladder's underside.

The heartweed needs one more thing: nitrogen. Veilstriders periodically kneel, folding their long legs like collapsing tent poles, and press the base of their bladder into the guano-rich nesting grounds of the small, burrowing creatures that live along the salt flats. It is an oddly intimate posture for such a towering animal.

## The Great Walk

Because the habitable twilight sways with the sun's apparent wobble, Veilstriders spend their entire lives in a slow, rhythmic migration. Over each 41-day cycle they walk roughly 200 kilometers toward the dayside, then 200 kilometers back toward the night. Herds of dozens or even hundreds move together, spaced evenly apart so they don't shade one another.

Too close to the dayside, the focused sunlight inside them grows intense enough to cook the heartweed, and the creatures cloud their gel with a milky pigment to diffuse the light. Too close to the nightside, the cold thickens their fluid and slows their movements to a crawl. Herds that misjudge the timing can be found frozen in place, perfectly preserved glass sculptures standing on the edge of the dark.

## Sound

Veilstriders are mostly quiet, but at the turning point of each migration, when the herd reverses direction, they produce a sound. By rhythmically contracting the bladder, they set the internal gel vibrating, creating a deep, resonant hum, something like a finger circling the rim of a wine glass, but far lower and impossibly long. A full herd humming together can be heard thirty kilometers away and seems to come from the ground itself.

# The Veshran Windstrider

## Its World

Veshra orbits a dim red dwarf and is **tidally locked**: one hemisphere bakes in endless day while the other lies frozen in permanent night. Between them runs the *Terminator Belt*, a ring of eternal twilight a few hundred kilometers wide where nearly all complex life exists. A ceaseless wind roars across this belt, rising off the scorching dayside and rushing toward the frozen dark.

The Windstrider lives its entire life walking into that wind.

## Anatomy

A mature Windstrider stands about **four meters tall** and weighs surprisingly little, around 60 kilograms, because most of its body is membrane and air.

- **The Sail:** Its most striking feature is a vast, translucent membrane stretched across a fan of hollow ribs, like a living kite. The membrane is a deep violet-black, which absorbs the weak red sunlight as efficiently as possible. Fine veins carry a copper-based fluid that gives the sail a faint bronze shimmer when the light catches it.
- **The Legs:** It walks on **three long, jointed legs** arranged in a tripod, so at least two feet always grip the ground. Each foot ends in a splayed, rootlike claw that anchors into soil or rock during violent gusts.
- **The Keel:** Beneath the sail hangs a dense, teardrop-shaped core that holds its organs and acts as ballast, keeping the creature upright in winds that would topple anything top-heavy.
- **No true head:** Its sensory organs are spread along the leading edge of the sail.

## How It Eats

The dayside's scorched surface sheds enormous clouds of spores, pollen, and microscopic drifting organisms, which the wind carries into the twilight. The Windstrider is a **filter feeder of the sky**. Its sail is lined with millions of sticky, hairlike cilia that catch drifting food. Ripples of muscle along the ribs sweep the catch down toward a slit-like mouth at the base of the keel.

It never needs to hunt. It only needs to face the wind and wait for the wind to feed it.

## Why It Never Stops Walking

The same wind that feeds the Windstrider also pushes it toward the lethal cold of the nightside. A resting Windstrider drifts backward, inch by inch, toward the dark. So it walks upwind, slowly and constantly, its whole life. Its gait is a deliberate three-beat rhythm: plant, lean, pull. To a human observer, a herd looks like a procession of dark sailing ships crawling across the twilight plains.

Herds travel in **staggered V-formations**, like migrating geese. Each animal shelters partly in the wake of the one ahead, and the lead position rotates so no single strider becomes exhausted.

## Senses

- **Infrared eyes:** A row of about twenty small, glossy black eyes lines the top edge of the sail. They see deep into the infrared, where most of the red dwarf's light falls, and can spot the warm bodies of predators at great distances.
- **Pressure sensing:** The sail itself is the main sense organ. It feels tiny shifts in wind pressure, which warn of approaching storms, sudden gusts, and obstacles ahead.
- **Taste on the wind:** The feeding cilia also sample airborne chemicals, so a Windstrider can "taste" a food-rich spore cloud kilometers before reaching it.

## Song

The hollow ribs of the sail are open at the tips. By tightening muscles around each rib, the Windstrider tunes the wind passing through them, producing **low, organ-like chords**. A herd on the move produces a constant shifting harmony that carries for many kilometers. Different chords seem to signal danger, rich feeding grounds, or a call to tighten formation. Travelers on Veshra describe the plains as never truly silent: there is always distant music on the wind.

## Life Cycle

1. **Seeding:** Adults release lightweight seed-pods, each wrapped in a tiny sail of its own. These deliberately travel *downwind*, tumbling toward the colder edge of the twilight.
2. **Sheltering:** Pods lodge in crevices and the lees of boulders, where the young grow for several years, rooted in place like plants and feeding on whatever drifts into their hollows.
3. **Awakening:** When its sail is large enough, the juvenile pulls its legs free and begins the walk upwind, eventually joining a passing herd.
4. **The Long Walk:** An adult may live 80 Veshran years and walk the equivalent of several times around Earth, all against the wind.

## Death

When a Windstrider grows too old to keep pace, it stops walking. Its legs release their grip, its sail fills, and the wind lifts it from the ground. It drifts slowly toward the nightside, where it freezes and settles onto the ice.

Over millennia, fields of preserved sails have built up at the edge of the dark, standing in the frozen wind like a forest of dark glass. Some still hum faintly as air passes through their hollow ribs, a final chord carried back toward the light.

# The Dawnwalkers of Keth

## The World

Keth is a rocky planet that turns very slowly, completing one rotation every 412 Earth days. As a result, its surface is divided into two hostile extremes. On the dayside, the ground bakes under a sun that hangs in the sky for months, reaching temperatures that boil water. On the nightside, months of darkness freeze the land into a brittle, glittering waste.

Between them lies the **terminator**, a narrow band of perpetual dawn a few dozen kilometers wide, where the temperature is mild and life can exist. Because the planet rotates, this band of dawn creeps steadily across the surface at about 3 kilometers per hour, roughly a human walking pace.

Anything that wants to live on Keth must keep up with it.

## The Creature

The **Dawnwalker** has spent its entire evolutionary history walking. It has never stopped, because stopping means death.

**Size and shape:** An adult stands about four meters tall at the shoulder. It has a long, narrow body slung between six slender, many-jointed legs. Its gait is a smooth, rippling wave, with legs lifting in sequence from back to front, so the body glides at an unchanging height. Over millions of years, Dawnwalkers have been shaped for endurance rather than speed. Their muscles are dense with slow-twitch fibers, and their joints are cushioned with fluid-filled pads that never wear down.

**The sails:** Along its back rises a row of tall, thin fins. These are folded membranes stretched between flexible spines, colored a deep wine-purple. They are photosynthetic. The sun on Keth always sits low on the horizon behind the walking herd, so the sails angle backward to catch the long, golden light. A Dawnwalker gets about a third of its energy this way. The rest comes from grazing. On cold "mornings," the sails flush with warm blood and act as radiators in reverse, soaking up heat.

**The face:** The front of the Dawnwalker always points toward the frozen night it walks into, so its head is built for darkness. It has four enormous eyes, each the size of a dinner plate, with reflective layers behind the retina that make them flash silver-green when light hits them. A pair of feathery sensory tendrils hangs below the jaw and sweeps the ground ahead, tasting the soil for thawing food.

**Skin:** Its hide is pale gray and leathery, covered in fine overlapping scales that can lie flat to shed heat or lift to trap insulating air. Older Dawnwalkers develop pale scars and patches from frostbite on their faces and sunburn on their hindquarters, a record of every time they drifted too far toward either edge.

## The Never-Ending Day

**Feeding:** The thin band of land at the edge of night is where the Dawnwalkers graze. As the ice thaws, dormant spores burst into life all at once. Within hours, the ground is carpeted in "flash-flora," fleshy, fast-growing plants in vivid blues and oranges that sprout, flower, and seed in just a few days before the advancing heat withers them. The Dawnwalkers eat as they walk, pulling up mouthfuls with their tendrils and never breaking stride. In return, the seeds pass through their gut and are deposited in their dung, spread across the planet in a continuous line.

**Sleeping:** A Dawnwalker cannot lie down, so it sleeps one half of its brain at a time, much like dolphins on Earth. A sleeping Dawnwalker walks a little slower, its sails droop, and it hums softly. The herd arranges itself so the sleepers walk in the middle, guided by the wakeful ones around them.

**The herd:** Dawnwalkers travel in herds of several hundred. They communicate through deep, rolling calls produced in resonating chambers inside their long chests, sounds that carry for kilometers across the still dawn air. Researchers studying the herds (in this imagined future) would notice that the herds seem to "sing" in long, repeating patterns. One completed circuit of the planet, one full rotation, appears to correspond to one complete "song." Each herd's song is slightly different.

## Birth and Death

A Dawnwalker gives birth while walking. The calf drops onto the soft, thawing ground wrapped in a thick, insulating membrane, and it has about two hours to stand and start walking before the herd moves too far ahead. The mother circles back, walking around and around her calf, singing to it, until it rises on six wobbly legs. Calves stay pressed to their mothers' sides for the first few circuits of the planet, sheltered beneath her sails.

Dawnwalkers can live for about thirty circuits, which is roughly thirty-four Earth years. As they age, they slow down. Year by year, an elder drifts toward the back of the herd, where the air is hotter and the food is gone. Eventually, it can no longer keep pace.

The herd doesn't abandon it all at once. The elder's closest companions slow down with it for as long as they safely can, singing, until they're forced to move on. Then the elder walks alone, steadily falling behind into the lengthening day, until the heat claims it.

Its bones remain on the dayside, bleached and scattered. Months later, the slow turn of the planet brings the night over them, then the dawn again, and a new herd passes by, grazing among the flowers that sprouted where the old one fell.

## Predators

The Dawnwalkers' main enemy is the **rimewait**, a flat, armored predator that survives the long night by burrowing into the ice and entering a deep, cold sleep. It wakes only when the dawn thaw reaches it, already in the path of an approaching herd. A rimewait bursts from the softening ground with no warning, seizing a Dawnwalker's legs in its jaws. This is why the herd's scouts, the wakeful adults at the very front, constantly sweep the ground with their tendrils, feeling for the faint warmth of a waking body beneath the ice.

---

The Dawnwalkers have walked around Keth millions of times. They've never seen the full blaze of noon or the depths of midnight. Their whole world is a single, endless sunrise, and they have spent their entire existence following it.

# The Lanternmoss Strider of Veyra

## The World

Veyra is a rocky planet orbiting an orange star. It spins so slowly that a single day lasts about 400 Earth days. Its long nights grow cold enough to freeze the shallow seas, and its long afternoons are hot enough to scorch exposed soil. Life survives by staying in the narrow band of mild dawn light that creeps across the surface at roughly the pace of a human walk.

The most remarkable creature to exploit this is the **Lanternmoss Strider**, an animal that spends its entire life walking toward the sunrise.

## Appearance

An adult Strider stands about six meters tall at the shoulder and weighs around twelve tons, but it looks less like an animal than like a hill that has decided to move. Its body is a broad, low dome supported by **eight stilt-like legs**, each ending in a splayed, three-toed foot padded with spongy cartilage that cushions every step on the endless march.

The dome is the Strider's defining feature. Its back is covered in a thick, living carpet of **lanternmoss**, a symbiotic photosynthetic organism that grows in shaggy golden-green layers up to half a meter deep. The moss feeds the Strider sugars through thousands of tiny root-channels that pierce its hide. In return, the Strider carries the moss perpetually into the gentle dawn light, keeping it out of both the killing night and the scorching noon. Neither can live without the other.

At night, or when the animal is alarmed, the moss gives off a soft bioluminescent glow in pulsing amber waves. From a distance, a herd of Striders crossing a plain looks like a procession of slow, breathing lanterns.

## Senses

The Strider has no distinct head. At the front of the dome sits a **sensory ridge**, a crescent of a dozen glossy black eye-spots tuned almost entirely to the horizon. The Strider's whole existence depends on one question: *where is the light coming from?* Its eyes detect the faint pre-dawn glow far below the horizon, so the animal can correct its heading even through dust storms.

Beneath the ridge hang two long, whiskery **feeler-tongues** that sweep the ground as it walks. They taste the soil for minerals the moss can't provide, especially phosphorus and iron, and pull up mineral-rich clays, which the Strider swallows in small mouthfuls.

## Behavior and the Long Circle

Striders never stop walking. A Strider that falls behind the dawn will slowly drift into the heat of the long day, where its moss will wither and the animal will starve. One that walks too fast will outpace the sunrise and freeze in the dark.

Because the dawn line moves fastest at the equator, Striders live at high latitudes, where the planet's circumference is smaller and the sunrise moves at a manageable walking pace. Over many generations, herds have worn deep, permanent trails into the bedrock: a great looping path around Veyra's northern polar region called **the Long Circle** by the scientists who study them. A single Strider may walk the Circle over a hundred times in its two-century lifespan.

They sleep in shifts while moving. Each half of the Strider's brain rests in turn, and the legs keep walking on a kind of reflexive autopilot while herd-mates bump gently against a dozing neighbor to keep it on course.

## Communication

Striders communicate through **light and sound**. Rippling patterns in the lanternmoss signal mood: slow, even pulses mean calm; rapid flickers mean danger. They also produce deep, resonant hums from air chambers inside the dome. These sounds are so low that they travel for kilometers through the ground and can be felt more than heard. A herd hums together almost constantly, a droning chorus that researchers have compared to a cathedral organ played underwater.

## Reproduction

Striders don't lay eggs or bear live young in the usual sense. Instead, an adult develops a **brood-pocket** within the moss on its back. A single offspring grows there for about four years, nourished by the parent's moss, before it is large enough to climb down and walk on its own.

A newly independent juvenile carries only a thin patch of moss "seeded" from its parent. As it grows, its garden spreads. Older Striders have been observed rubbing against younger ones, sharing moss strains with them, a behavior that resembles grooming but may actually be an exchange of genetic heritage between symbiotic lineages.

## Death

When a Strider grows too old to keep pace, it slowly falls behind the herd and drifts into the deepening day. Eventually it lies down and does not rise. The moss on its back, sensing the change, releases a cloud of spores before dying, and the winds of the dawn line carry them forward to the herd ahead.

Scientists on Veyra say that every Strider walking the Long Circle carries, in some sense, a small piece of every Strider that walked before it.

# The Windharp of Tessaly

## The World

Tessaly is a rocky planet tidally locked to a dim red dwarf star. One hemisphere bakes in permanent daylight, and the other is locked in endless frozen night. Between them lies the **Ember Belt**, a ring of perpetual sunset a few hundred kilometers wide, where the star hangs forever on the horizon like a swollen coal.

Because the dayside heats the air and the nightside chills it, a ceaseless wind flows across the surface from the dark toward the light. It never stops, and it rarely changes direction. Everything that lives in the Ember Belt has evolved around that wind. The most remarkable of these creatures is the **windharp**.

## Appearance

An adult windharp stands about four meters tall and looks like a cross between a tree, a spider, and a musical instrument.

- **The Body:** A teardrop-shaped central body, roughly the size of a large barrel, is covered in overlapping black plates. Under Tessaly's weak red light, plants and animals alike tend toward black or deep violet to absorb every possible photon. The plates have a faint oily iridescence, shimmering bronze when the light catches them.

- **The Legs:** Six long, jointed legs splay outward and end in fibrous "rootfeet" that the windharp drives into the soil. Most of the time it stands anchored and motionless, braced against the wind like a tent pitched in a gale.

- **The Strings:** Its defining feature rises from its back: a fan-shaped frame of two curved, horn-like spars with dozens of fine, silky filaments stretched between them. These **strings** are sticky, elastic, and nearly invisible at a distance. The windharp always faces its frame into the wind, toward the night.

- **The Eyes:** Clustered along the front of its body are eight large, glossy eyes tuned mostly to infrared. To a windharp, the world glows with heat: the warm horizon, the cold dark behind it, and the faint thermal shimmer of other living things.

## Feeding

The windharp is a filter feeder of the air. The wind blowing out of the nightside carries a constant drizzle of drifting life: hardy spores, wind-borne seeds, tiny gliding insects, and clumps of frozen microbes that thaw as they reach the twilight warmth.

These particles stick to the harp's strings. Every few hours, the windharp slowly draws a comb-like mouthpart up along each filament, scraping the strings clean and swallowing the harvest. A well-placed windharp in a strong wind corridor can feed for weeks without taking a single step.

## The Song

As the wind passes through the strings, they vibrate and produce sound: low, eerie, organ-like tones that carry for kilometers in Tessaly's thick atmosphere.

But windharps are not passive instruments. Muscles at the base of each string let the creature adjust its tension, and so its pitch. Windharps "sing" by tuning their strings, turning the wind itself into their voice. Each individual has a recognizable chord, a sonic signature that works like a name.

When a herd of windharps stands across a ridgeline, their combined voices create a vast, shifting harmony. Researchers who have heard recordings describe it as unsettling and beautiful, like a cathedral choir humming underwater. The song carries information: warnings of predators, the location of rich wind corridors, and courtship displays in which males hold sustained, perfectly pure intervals for hours at a time.

## Life Cycle

Windharps begin life as tiny seed-like larvae, each wrapped in a feathery membrane. Adults release them into the wind during rare reversals, brief storms when the airflow stutters and swirls. The larvae drift for weeks, sometimes crossing hundreds of kilometers before they settle.

A juvenile spends its first years low to the ground with a small, crude harp, producing only thin, whistling notes. As it grows, its frame widens and its strings multiply. Windharps can live for over two centuries, and the oldest develop enormous harps with deep, resonant voices. Younger harps seem to orient toward these elders and harmonize with them.

## Dangers and Defenses

The windharp's greatest threat isn't a predator but its own star. Red dwarfs are prone to violent **flares**, sudden bursts of radiation that can scorch exposed life. Windharps sense the pre-flare change in the star's infrared glow minutes in advance. When it comes, the whole herd folds in unison: strings retract into grooves along the spars, the frame collapses flat against the body, and the creature hunkers down beneath its armored plates. A landscape that was singing a moment before falls completely silent.

Their main predator is the **gloamcrawler**, a low, many-legged ambush hunter that uses the windharps' song to locate them. To counter it, windharps have a final trick: they can deliberately detune their strings into a harsh, dissonant shriek that disorients the gloamcrawler's sensitive hearing and alerts every windharp within range.

## Why It Matters

To anyone standing in the Ember Belt, the windharps would be the defining feature of the landscape: tall dark silhouettes against a bloodred horizon, strings glinting faintly, the whole world humming with a slow, endless chord. They are a creature shaped entirely by one unchanging fact of their planet: the wind always blows, and so the windharp has learned to eat it, sing with it, and live by it.

Rising from its back is a cluster of thirty to sixty **hollow tubes**, each a different length. The shortest are no taller than a hand. The longest can reach four meters. At the base of every tube is a ring of muscle that works like a valve, opening or sealing the pipe at will.

These tubes are the creature's mouth, lungs, and voice all at once:

- **Feeding:** The inner walls are coated in a sticky, slowly circulating mucus. As wind rushes through, aeroplankton sticks to the lining, and tiny hair-like cilia carry it down into the digestive chamber beneath the dome.
- **Breathing:** Gas exchange happens through the thin tissue lining the tubes.
- **Sound:** Wind passing over the tube openings produces tones, exactly like blowing across a bottle.

Beneath the shell, dozens of root-like **anchor tendrils** grip deep into cracks in the bedrock. These also serve as the windharp's ears, picking up vibrations through the ground. It has no eyes, only patches of light-sensitive tissue along the rim of its shell that tell day from night.

## Behavior: The Choirs

Windharps live in loose groups called **choirs**, spaced tens of meters apart across the plains. By opening and closing their valves, they turn the wind into chords, shifting harmonies that roll across the landscape for kilometers.

The song is not decoration. It is language:

- **Storm warning.** When a dust storm approaches, the windward windharps feel the pressure change first. They shift to a sharp, dissonant cluster of notes, and the signal ripples down the choir. Each windharp seals its tubes against the abrasive dust.
- **Feeding reports.** Rich bands of aeroplankton produce a bright, rising motif, prompting others to open their longest pipes, which catch more air.
- **Danger.** The windharp's main predator is the *shroudmoth*, a flat, gliding animal that settles over a tube and drills through the softer tissue at its base. When one lands, the victim emits a sudden, stuttering silence, and its neighbors answer with a low drone that seems to confuse the shroudmoth's own vibration-sensing organs.

## Life Cycle

Young windharps look nothing like their parents. They are born as **tumblers**: light, spherical, hollow shells about the size of a melon, released in great numbers during the spring winds. They roll and bounce across the plains for years, sometimes circling the planet more than once, feeding passively as air whistles through the small holes in their shells.

As a tumbler grows, its holes lengthen inward into proto-tubes, and it begins to develop a **pitch**, a dominant tone unique to its shape.

Then comes the most remarkable part of its life. When a tumbler rolls past a choir, it listens. If the choir's harmony has a *gap*, a missing note left by a member that died, and the tumbler's own pitch fills that gap, it stops. It sends out its tendrils, anchors to the stone, and begins growing its adult tubes. Choirs are therefore not families. They are assemblies of strangers, each chosen by the sound it was missing.

## Old Age and Death

Windharps can live for several centuries. Over time their longest tubes crack and are regrown, and their voices slowly deepen. The oldest members of a choir produce tones so low they are felt more than heard.

When a windharp dies, its valves relax and fall open for good. The shell remains, and the wind still plays through it, producing a steady, unchanging chord that no longer responds to anything. Human colonists call these **ghost notes**. The living choir gradually reshapes its harmony around the dead member, until the shell erodes and a gap opens in the song.

Eventually, a tumbler rolls by, hears the silence where a note should be, and stays.

## A Footnote From the First Survey

The first robotic landers on Kessra recorded faint, layered tones drifting across the plains. Mission scientists spent eleven months assuming they were hearing wind erosion in porous rock. Only when a lander's microphone captured a choir changing key moments before a storm hit did anyone realize the planet had been singing back.

# The Hollowsinger of Vesh

## The World

Vesh orbits a dim red dwarf so closely that it is **tidally locked**: one hemisphere bakes under a sun that never sets, and the other lies in permanent, frozen night. Between them runs a narrow ring of eternal twilight called the **Seam**, a band a few hundred kilometers wide where the sun hangs forever on the horizon like a swollen coal. Nearly all complex life on Vesh lives here.

Vesh's orbit is slightly eccentric, so the planet *wobbles* (astronomers call it libration). Over a cycle of about forty Earth days, the sun creeps a little higher in the sky, then sinks back. The habitable zone slides back and forth across the land like a slow tide of light.

The Hollowsinger has built its entire existence around following that tide.

---

## Appearance

An adult Hollowsinger stands **nine to eleven meters tall**, though most of that height is leg. It walks on **six long, jointed stilts**, each ending in a broad, splayed foot of rubbery pads that spreads its weight across the soft, frost-heaved soil of the Seam. The legs move in a slow, rolling ripple, front to back, so the creature seems to *flow* rather than walk.

Slung between the legs is the body: a long, keel-shaped torso about the size of a small boat, tapering at both ends. Its hide is made of **overlapping translucent plates**, like layers of smoky quartz. When the low sun shines through them, you can faintly see the shapes of organs inside, glowing a deep amber.

The creature's most striking feature is its back. It is covered in a thick, shaggy **mantle of near-black fronds** that ripple in the wind like a living cloak. They aren't part of the Hollowsinger at all (more on that below).

There is no distinct head. At the front of the body, a cluster of **four flexible feeding tubes** hangs down like an elephant's trunk split into fingers. Above them sit two deep, heat-sensing pits that give the creature an oddly mournful, hollow-eyed look.

---

## The Mantle: A Garden on Its Back

The black fronds are a **symbiotic plant-like organism** the Veshan biologists call *nightweave*. Under a red dwarf's dim, infrared-heavy light, the most efficient photosynthetic pigments are dark, absorbing nearly every wavelength they can catch. So the nightweave is black as soot.

The relationship benefits both partners:
- **The nightweave** gets mobility. The Hollowsinger carries it constantly into the best light, keeping it in the Seam's sweet spot as the twilight band shifts.
- **The Hollowsinger** gets sugar. Fine root-threads from the nightweave penetrate the host's back plates and feed it a steady trickle of nutrients.

A Hollowsinger can't survive on its mantle alone, but the mantle carries it through lean times. A healthy herd moving across the plain looks like a procession of walking, wind-tossed hillsides.

---

## Feeding

Along the Seam, meltwater streams trickle out of the glaciers of the night side, carrying rich mineral silt and colonies of microorganisms. The Hollowsinger wades into these streams and lowers its four feeding tubes, which **vacuum up the mineral slurry**. Inside, a series of internal chambers sorts and digests the microbes and holds the minerals, which the creature passes along to its nightweave as fertilizer.

It also grazes on **frostmoss**, a crunchy, crystalline growth that crusts the shaded sides of rocks. Hollowsingers can be heard from a long way off crunching it, a sound like someone walking on fresh snow.

---

## The Song

The Hollowsinger's name comes from its bones.

Its skeleton is **hollow and chambered**, more like a set of organ pipes than a frame. By forcing air through these chambers, it produces **infrasound**: deep, rumbling tones around 5–10 hertz, too low for human ears to hear. You would *feel* them instead, as a pressure in your chest and a faint buzzing in your teeth.

These calls carry **hundreds of kilometers** through Vesh's thick atmosphere. Herds use them to:
- **Coordinate migration**, signaling when the light is shifting and it is time to move.
- **Warn of danger**, especially the violent windstorms that pour off the night side when cold air collapses toward the warmer Seam.
- **Find each other.** Every Hollowsinger has a unique tonal signature, and individuals separated for years can recognize one another across a continent.

When a whole herd sings at once, the ground itself hums. Smaller creatures of the Seam have evolved to read these vibrations, scattering or gathering depending on the chord.

---

## Life Cycle

Hollowsingers don't lay eggs or give live birth in the usual sense. Young begin as **small buds** that form on the creature's back, nestled deep inside the nightweave. For the first year, the calf lives entirely in the mantle, fed by both its parent and the fronds around it, rocking gently through the dusk as the adult walks.

When the calf is roughly the size of a large dog, it drops to the ground on spindly legs and begins to walk beneath its parent, sheltered by the canopy of legs. It carries a few strands of nightweave with it. These are cuttings from its parent's mantle that will grow into its own garden over the next several decades.

Hollowsingers can live **for centuries**. The oldest individuals have mantles so thick and heavy that smaller creatures nest in them: burrowing insects, tiny gliding lizards, entire microecosystems riding along on a giant's back.

---

## Death and the Singing Groves

When a Hollowsinger dies, its soft tissues decompose quickly, but its hollow bones remain, often still standing upright, locked in place by its final stance. Wind passing over the bones makes them **moan and whistle**, sometimes for hundreds of years.

These skeletal remains are called **singing groves**. Herds often go out of their way to pass them, slowing down and answering the bones' tones with their own low calls. Whether this is grief, memory, or simple navigation (the groves make excellent landmarks), no one knows.

Other species shelter among the bones, and the nightweave left behind sometimes takes root in the soil, turning the grave into a small black thicket. Over time, the Seam becomes dotted with these quiet, humming monuments, each one marking a place where a giant once stopped walking.

---

## A Glimpse

Picture standing on a ridge at the edge of the Seam. To your left, the night side is a wall of blue-black ice under a sky full of stars. To your right, the sun sits fat and red on the horizon, painting everything in rust and copper.

Across the plain below, a line of dark shapes moves slowly through the twilight: tall, swaying, impossibly long-legged, their shaggy black backs rippling in the wind. You can't hear them. But you feel the ground thrumming under your boots, a deep, slow pulse, like the whole world has a heartbeat.

The Hollowsingers are calling to one another. The light is shifting, and it is time to walk.

# The Vaelith of Kerrow's Edge

## The World

Kerrow is a rocky planet tidally locked to a dim red dwarf star. One hemisphere bakes in endless noon, and the other is frozen in eternal night. Between them runs the **Terminator**, a ring of perpetual twilight a few hundred kilometers wide where the temperature is mild enough for liquid water. Almost all complex life lives in this narrow band, and the largest creature there is the **Vaelith**.

## Appearance

A grown Vaelith stands about four meters at the shoulder and stretches nearly ten meters from snout to tail. Six long, many-jointed legs carry its body like a slow-moving table, giving it the unhurried, swaying gait of a walking tree.

Its back is its most striking feature: a dense mane of **feathery fronds**, black with a violet sheen. The fronds are photosynthetic, but because Kerrow's sun gives off mostly deep red and infrared light, they are dark rather than green, built to absorb every scrap of energy from the low, never-moving sun. When the wind blows across a herd, the fronds ripple like a field of black wheat, and in the right light they shimmer faintly purple, like oil on water.

Its skin is thick, leathery, and slate-gray, patterned with pale, branching lines that resemble frost or river deltas. No two Vaelith share the same pattern, and herd members seem to recognize each other by it.

## Senses

The Vaelith has **three eyes**, arranged for life on a world where light always comes from one direction:

- **One large sun-eye**, set high on the head, always turned toward the dayside horizon. It is enormous and glassy, adapted to read subtle shifts in the dim red glow, and it helps the Vaelith keep its fronds angled correctly.
- **Two small night-eyes**, on the back of the skull and facing the darkness. They are extraordinarily sensitive, and they watch for the faint bioluminescent flickers of predators approaching from the nightside.

Its feet end in wide, spongy pads threaded with fine filaments, almost like roots. With every step the Vaelith "tastes" the soil, sensing minerals, moisture, and the vibrations of other creatures moving nearby.

## Voice

Inside its barrel-shaped chest is a hollow **resonance chamber** lined with taut membranes. By forcing air through it, the Vaelith produces deep, droning songs, mostly too low for human ears to hear. Kerrow's atmosphere is thick, so these infrasonic calls can carry hundreds of kilometers along the Terminator, and separated herds stay in contact across vast distances. To a human visitor, a singing herd would feel less like a sound and more like a vibration in the ribs, along with an unexplained sense of melancholy.

## Diet and Daily Life

The Vaelith is half animal and half garden. Its fronds supply much of its energy, but not enough for a body that size, so it also grazes on the low, crusty mats of lichen-like organisms that carpet the twilight plains, scraping them up with a broad, bony lower lip.

Temperature control is a constant concern. When it grows too warm, a Vaelith turns its fronds edge-on to the sun and faces the cold night winds. When it grows too cold, it fans its fronds wide toward the light. A resting herd looks like a slowly rotating field of sails, each animal adjusting its angle by degrees.

## Predators and Defense

The Vaelith's main enemy is the **Skeln**, a pack hunter from the nightside. Skeln are lean, pale, and nearly blind, and they hunt by sensing body heat. They creep in from the darkness in groups of five or six, trying to separate a young or weak Vaelith from the herd.

When threatened, a Vaelith shakes its fronds violently and releases a dense cloud of **cold spores**, tiny particles that absorb heat as they drift. The cloud scrambles the Skeln's thermal senses, effectively making the herd vanish. Under cover of the spore fog, the adults close ranks around the young and lash out with their heavy forelegs.

## Life Cycle

Vaelith do not lay eggs or give live birth in the usual sense. Instead, an adult **buds** its young from swellings along its flanks. Each calf grows attached to its parent for several months, nourished directly through shared tissue, before detaching as a small, wobbly copy of the adult, its frond-mane still short and soft.

Kerrow's orbit has a slight wobble, so the Terminator shifts back and forth over a cycle of decades. Vaelith herds migrate with it, following ancient routes their ancestors walked for millions of years.

## The Final Stillness

The most remarkable part of a Vaelith's life is its end. When an elder grows too old to keep up with the herd, it stops walking. It chooses a spot, often a hilltop or a place where the soil tastes rich, and plants its feet. Over the following months the filaments in its footpads burrow deep into the ground, its legs stiffen into trunks, and its fronds grow larger and wilder.

## The World

Keth-Ora is a tidally locked planet orbiting a dim red dwarf. One hemisphere bakes in permanent daylight, and the other freezes in endless night. Life clusters in the **Twilight Band**, a ring of perpetual dusk where the sun hangs forever on the horizon, swollen and crimson. Hot winds from the dayside rush constantly toward the cold nightside, and the landscape is a vast expanse of shallow brine flats, salt pillars, and mineral crusts.

The Veilwalker lives here.

## Appearance

At first glance, a Veilwalker looks like a drifting tent of stained glass on stilts. It stands about six meters tall, but its body is surprisingly small: a teardrop-shaped core roughly the size of a large dog, suspended high above the ground.

**Legs:** Six impossibly thin legs, each jointed in four places, hold the body aloft. They are made of a dense, silica-reinforced material resembling smoky quartz, and they ring faintly like tapped crystal when the creature walks. Each leg ends in a splayed, flexible pad that spreads its weight across the soft salt crust.

**The Veil:** The creature's most striking feature is a vast, translucent membrane that unfurls from ridges along its back. Fully extended, it spans nearly fifteen meters. The veil is threaded with branching veins of deep violet and black pigment, tuned to absorb the red, infrared-heavy light of Keth-Ora's sun. When backlit by the low sun, a Veilwalker glows like a cathedral window.

**The Core:** The central body is armored in overlapping pale plates, slightly iridescent, like the inside of an oyster shell. Beneath it hangs a cluster of long, delicate feeding tendrils that trail across the ground.

**Eyes:** It has no eyes in the traditional sense. Instead, dozens of tiny pits dot the edges of the veil. Each is sensitive to heat and light direction, giving the creature a wide, low-resolution awareness of its surroundings.

## How It Lives

**Sailing and Walking:** The Veilwalker is part plant, part animal, and part sailboat. It angles its veil to catch the endless dayside wind, letting the breeze push it across the flats while its legs stride lightly, mostly steering and balancing rather than propelling. A herd moving across the brine looks like a slow regatta of glowing sails.

**Feeding:** Energy comes from two sources. The veil photosynthesizes using the dim red light, but this alone isn't enough. The trailing tendrils sweep the ground for mineral-rich crusts and the mats of microbial life growing in the brine pools. The tendrils secrete a mild acid, dissolve the crust, and absorb the slurry.

**Temperature Control:** Because the dayside edge is scorching and the nightside edge is lethal, the Veilwalker must stay within a narrow band. If it drifts too far toward the heat, it folds its veil to reduce exposure. If it strays toward the cold, it spreads the veil wide and turns it broadside to the sun like a solar panel.

## Communication

Veilwalkers are social and travel in loose herds of twenty to forty. They communicate in two ways:

- **Color shifting:** Specialized cells in the veil can rapidly change pigment, sending ripples of violet, amber, and pale blue across the membrane. A calm herd displays slow, wave-like pulses. Alarm triggers sudden flashes of bright gold.
- **Leg-song:** By flexing the crystalline joints of their legs, they produce low, chiming tones that carry for kilometers across the flats. On still days (rare, but they happen), whole herds can be heard harmonizing, a sound like distant wind chimes played underwater.

## Life Cycle

Veilwalkers reproduce during the **Long Calm**, a period every few years when the planet's slightly elliptical orbit weakens the winds. Herds gather at ancient salt pillars, where pairs intertwine their veils in elaborate color displays.

Afterward, the parent anchors a cluster of glassy seed-pods to the pillar's base. The young, called *sparklings*, hatch as tiny, legless jelly-like creatures that drift in the brine pools for their first year, feeding on microbes. Only later do they grow their legs, climb out of the water, and slowly unfurl their first small, colorless veils. Pigment develops over time, and no two adults have the same vein pattern, so each one's veil is as unique as a fingerprint.

## Place in the Ecosystem

Veilwalkers are a keystone species. Their acidic feeding breaks down mineral crusts, releasing nutrients that feed the brine-pool microbes. Their shed veils, which they molt every season, settle on the flats as thin, glittering sheets that small scavengers consume and burrowing creatures use as shelter.

Their main predator is the **Skarn**, a low, flat ambusher that buries itself in the salt and waits to snap a leg. This is why Veilwalkers walk so delicately, testing every step, and why a herd's leg-song suddenly falls silent when one of them senses vibration beneath the crust.

# The Tethered Veilwing

**Home world:** Ouris, a tidally locked planet orbiting a dim red dwarf. One hemisphere faces the sun in permanent noon, and the other lies in endless night. Between them runs the *Gloaming*, a ring of perpetual twilight where most life clusters. Because hot air rises on the day side and rushes toward the cold night side, Ouris has a constant, planet-wide wind that never stops blowing.

The Veilwing has built its entire existence around that wind.

---

## Appearance

An adult Veilwing looks like a living kite. Its main body is a broad, diamond-shaped membrane up to **12 meters across**, thin as paper but remarkably tough, stretched over a lattice of hollow, flexible spars. The membrane is **velvety black**. Ouris's red sun emits most of its energy in deep red and infrared, so the Veilwing's photosynthetic pigments evolved to absorb every wavelength it can get, leaving nothing to reflect.

Hanging from the underside of the membrane is the **keel**, a dense, teardrop-shaped core about the size of a large dog. It contains the creature's digestive organs, nervous center, and reproductive tissue. From the keel descends the Veilwing's most remarkable feature, the **tether**.

## The Tether

The tether is a single living cord, often **200 to 400 meters long**, that anchors the Veilwing to the ground. It is part root, part spine, and part nervous system:

- **At the bottom**, it splits into a mass of burrowing filaments that dig into rock crevices and soil, drawing up water and dissolved minerals.
- **Along its length**, fluids are pumped upward through hollow channels, so a Veilwing "drinks" from hundreds of meters below.
- **Throughout**, nerve fibers transmit vibration, letting the creature sense movement on the ground, changes in wind tension, and approaching threats.

A Veilwing in flight constantly adjusts the angle of its membrane, the way a sailor trims a sail, to hold its position against the gale.

## Feeding

Photosynthesis alone isn't enough to power a creature this large in such weak light, so the Veilwing supplements its diet by **filter-feeding from the wind**. The day side releases enormous clouds of spores, pollen-like seeds, and tiny airborne organisms called *driftmotes*, and the endless wind carries them all toward the night.

The leading edge of the Veilwing's membrane is lined with fine, sticky cilia that comb this "aerial plankton" from the passing air. Captured food is swept along grooves in the membrane toward the keel, where it is digested. A healthy Veilwing positioned in a rich wind current is essentially a sail that eats.

## Senses and Communication

Veilwings have no eyes in the conventional sense. Instead, they have patches of **heat-sensitive tissue** across the membrane that detect infrared, allowing them to "see" the warm day side, the cold night side, and warm-bodied creatures nearby.

They communicate by **singing through their tethers**. By tightening or loosening muscles along the cord, a Veilwing makes it hum in the wind like the string of an instrument. These low, droning tones travel through the air and the ground. A large colony of Veilwings, called a **choir**, produces a constant, shifting chord that can be heard for kilometers. Researchers on Ouris would likely find that changes in the choir's pitch warn of storms, predators, or the arrival of rich spore clouds.

## Life Cycle

1. **Seedling:** Veilwings begin as tiny, untethered membranes no bigger than a hand, released by the millions during storms. They tumble freely on the wind, feeding on driftmotes.
2. **Wanderer:** Most are eaten or blown into the frozen night side. Survivors grow for months while drifting, until they're large enough to settle.
3. **Anchoring:** A maturing Veilwing drops a thin filament that drags along the ground until it catches. It then sinks in, thickens, and becomes the tether. Once anchored, the creature never moves again unless something goes wrong.
4. **Adult:** Anchored Veilwings may live for **centuries**, their tethers growing thicker each year. Their roots slowly break down rock, creating soil around their anchor points.
5. **Release:** In the planet's rare great storms, old Veilwings sometimes deliberately **sever their own tethers**, letting the wind carry them far across the Gloaming. As they fly, they scatter seedlings from pouches along the membrane. They eventually fall, and their bodies become feasts for ground-dwellers.

## Ecology

Veilwings are a keystone species in the Gloaming:

- **The tethers form vertical forests.** Small, six-limbed climbers called *spirelings* live their whole lives on the cords, grazing on lichen-like growths.
- **They have predators.** The most feared is the *coilmaw*, a long-bodied ground hunter that climbs tethers to reach the keel. A Veilwing's defense is to violently snap its tether, whipping the climber off. Choirs sing warnings to one another when coilmaws approach.
- **They shape the landscape.** Where Veilwing colonies anchor, their roots create fertile ground, and their shadows offer cool shelter. Seen from orbit, a choir looks like a field of black diamonds floating above the twilight.

# The Veyran Hollowsinger

## The World It Inhabits

Veyra is a rocky planet locked in orbit around a dim red dwarf star. One hemisphere faces the sun in permanent, scorching noon, and the other lies in endless frozen night. Between them runs the **Terminator Belt**, a ring of perpetual twilight a few hundred kilometers wide where liquid water and life can exist. A constant river of wind pours through this zone, flowing from the hot dayside toward the cold nightside, and it never stops.

The Hollowsinger is built entirely around that wind.

## Appearance

An adult stands about six meters tall. Its body is a tapering vertical column, a little like a living bassoon, supported on **three jointed legs** spaced evenly around its base. It has no front or back. It can walk in any direction, and it moves with a slow, rotating gait in which each leg swings around the others, so the creature seems to pirouette across the landscape.

Its hide is **matte black**, like most life on Veyra. Under a red dwarf's weak, reddish light, organisms evolved to absorb every photon they can, so the plains of the Terminator Belt look like charcoal velvet. Up close, the Hollowsinger's skin has a fine texture of overlapping plates, each edged in faint copper.

The most striking feature is the column itself. It is **hollow**, divided inside into a series of resonating chambers, and its surface is perforated with dozens of slits that the creature can open and close with rings of muscle.

## The Song

As the endless wind passes through its body, the Hollowsinger produces sound. By adjusting its slits, much as a musician fingers a flute, it controls pitch, volume, and rhythm. Most of the sound is **infrasonic**, far below human hearing, and it carries for dozens of kilometers across the open plains.

A human standing among a herd would hear only a faint, eerie moaning but would *feel* the rest as a pressure in the chest and a vibration in the teeth. To the Hollowsingers, it is language. They use it to:

- Keep scattered herds coordinated across vast distances
- Warn of approaching dust storms or predators
- Court mates through long, slowly evolving duets that can last for days

Older individuals have wider chambers and deeper voices, and younger animals appear to defer to them.

## Senses

Hollowsingers have no conventional eyes. Instead, a band of **infrared-sensitive pits** circles the upper column, giving them a 360-degree thermal view of the world. In the dim red light, warmth is more informative than color: they can see the heat of other creatures, the warm shadows of the dayside, and the cold edge of the night.

They also "hear" through their legs. Sensory pads in their three feet detect ground vibrations, so in a sense they listen to the land as much as to each other.

## Feeding

Hollowsingers are grazers. They eat **ashmoss**, a black, photosynthetic mat that carpets the twilight plains. At the base of the column is a mouth that unrolls a long, ribbon-like tongue lined with abrasive ridges. The creature sweeps it in slow spirals, scraping up moss as it rotates. Herds leave distinctive curling patterns across the plains, like enormous fingerprints.

## Flare Defense

Red dwarf stars are violent. Without warning, Veyra's sun can erupt in flares that flood the surface with radiation. Hollowsingers sense the sudden spike in heat and light, and in seconds every member of the herd **unfurls a silvery, reflective membrane** from a ridge near the top of its column, opening it like an umbrella.

It is one of the most remarkable sights on Veyra: an entire herd of black towers turning brilliant silver at once, flashing in the red light until the flare passes.

## Life Cycle

Hollowsingers reproduce by releasing **wind-seeds**: small, papery juveniles with membranes that act like kites. Launched into the constant gale, they are carried toward the nightside, sometimes hundreds of kilometers.

Those that land near the cold edge put down legs and begin growing, feeding on hardy frost-lichens. Then they spend their entire youth **walking back against the wind**, toward the warmer heart of the Terminator Belt. This journey can take decades. Only the strongest survive it, and by the time they arrive, their chambers have grown large enough for them to join the chorus of an adult herd.

Hollowsingers can live for **several centuries**.

## Death and Afterlife

When a Hollowsinger grows very old, it stops walking. Its legs sink into the ground and slowly fuse with the soil, and the creature dies standing. Its body doesn't fall. The hard outer plates remain upright as a hollow tower, and the wind keeps passing through it.

These dead towers go on **singing**, though with fixed, unchanging notes. Over time, whole fields of them form across the plains, called "choirs" by anyone who might one day visit, each humming its single, frozen chord into the twilight.

The towers also become shelter. Small creatures nest in their chambers, ashmoss grows thick around their bases, and living herds often linger near them. It may be coincidence, or it may be that the young are listening to the voices of their ancestors.

# The Veyth Glasswader

## Its World

Veyth is a rocky planet tidally locked to a dim red dwarf. One hemisphere bakes in permanent daylight, and the other is frozen in endless night. Between them lies the **Ribbon**, a narrow band of perpetual twilight where liquid water can exist. Veyth's orbit is slightly elliptical, so the planet wobbles. Over each 19-day year, the sun creeps about 40 kilometers toward the night side and then drifts back. The Ribbon's shallow brine flats are constantly shifting between scorching light and killing frost.

The glasswader has evolved to walk with the light.

## Appearance

An adult glasswader stands about four meters tall, but most of that height is legs. It has **six stilt-like limbs**, each jointed in three places and ending in a broad, splayed pad webbed with rubbery skin. The pads spread its weight across soft salt-crust and mud. The legs are dark bronze, armored with overlapping plates that resist the corrosive brine.

The body is a compact, egg-shaped torso slung low between the legs. Its most striking feature rises from its back: the **lens-sail**, a tall, curved fin of transparent, gel-filled tissue, crystal-clear and faintly amber, shaped like a ship's sail. Beneath the sail, the skin of the back is packed with deep violet symbiotic microbes that photosynthesize using the red dwarf's weak, infrared-heavy light.

The sail works as a living magnifying glass. Muscles at its base flex and reshape the gel, focusing scattered twilight onto the symbiont bed below. A glasswader standing at rest slowly tracks the low sun with its sail, like a sunflower made of glass.

## Senses

The glasswader has no eyes in the conventional sense. Instead, a ring of **eleven pit organs** encircles the front of its torso. Each is a shallow cup lined with heat-sensitive tissue that can detect temperature differences of a fraction of a degree. In a world lit mostly by infrared, the creature "sees" warmth: the glow of the sun-side horizon, the heat of other animals, the cold shadows where frost is advancing.

Its foot-pads are also extraordinarily sensitive to vibration. Through the brine-soaked ground, a glasswader can feel the footsteps of its herd kilometers away, as well as the subtle cracking sound of salt crust freezing, an early warning that the night is encroaching.

## Feeding

Photosynthesis provides only about half of its energy. For the rest, the glasswader grazes on **mat-weed**, a slimy carpet of microbial colonies that blooms in the shallow pools. It feeds by lowering a long, flexible proboscis from beneath its torso and sweeping it across the water, scraping and sucking up the mats. Comb-like plates inside the proboscis filter out salt crystals and grit, which it expels in rhythmic, sneezing bursts.

## Behavior and Migration

Glasswaders live in loose herds of twenty to sixty. Their lives follow the planet's wobble. As the terminator drifts, the herd drifts with it, walking slowly and steadily to stay in the narrow sweet spot where light is strong enough to feed their symbionts but not strong enough to boil the shallow pools.

They communicate through **low, resonant hums** produced by forcing air through chambers in the torso. These sounds travel far through Veyth's thick atmosphere. When a herd changes direction at the end of the drift cycle, the whole group erupts into a rising, overlapping chorus that can last for hours. Researchers might call it the "turning song."

## Reproduction

Glasswaders lay eggs in the warmest pools at the sun-side edge of their range. Each egg is a hard, mirrored sphere that reflects excess light and keeps the embryo from overheating. Parents don't stay. Instead, the eggs are timed so the hatchlings emerge just as the terminator swings back toward them, meeting the next herd's arrival. Juveniles are born with stubby legs and a tiny, cloudy sail. They are adopted by whatever herd passes through, so a glasswader's family is defined by where it walks, not by who laid it.

## Predators and Dangers

The greatest threat is the **frostline**. A glasswader that falls behind, through injury or age, will be overtaken by the advancing cold. Its symbionts die first, turning the violet back pale gray, and the animal soon follows.

The main predator is the **skerrow**, a low, flat, many-limbed hunter that hides in the cold shadows on the night side of the herd. Skerrows are nearly invisible to heat-sensing pits because they keep their bodies chilled. They strike at legs, hoping to cripple a glasswader and let the cold finish the job. In response, herds travel with their oldest and largest members on the night-side flank, stamping in rhythm to detect anything moving in the frozen dark.

## In Death

When a glasswader dies, its lens-sail often survives long after the body decays. The gel slowly hardens into a clear, glassy slab. Across the Ribbon, these fallen sails litter the brine flats like scattered windows. Ancient migration routes can be traced by following lines of them stretching across the twilight, each one still faintly catching the low red sun.

The Lanternback Drifter lives on **Oreth**, a tidally locked planet orbiting a dim red dwarf. One hemisphere faces its sun in permanent, scorching day; the other lies in eternal night. The Drifter lives in the **Twilight Band**, a narrow ring of perpetual dusk between the two, where violet-orange light slants low across the horizon and winds roar constantly from the hot side to the cold.

Oreth's atmosphere is roughly three times denser than Earth's, and its gravity is only about 60% as strong. Together these make the air thick enough to "swim" through, and much of Oreth's life has taken to the sky.

A mature Drifter resembles a cross between a manta ray, a jellyfish, and a paper lantern. Its body is a broad, translucent **canopy membrane** up to eight meters across, stretched over a lattice of hollow, bamboo-like ribs. The membrane is thin enough that the dim red sunlight passes through it, giving the creature a soft rosy glow by day.

Along the ridge of its back runs a row of **bioluminescent chambers**, a dozen or more bulbous sacs that pulse with cold blue-green light. These "lanterns" give the species its name.

Beneath the canopy hang dozens of **trailing filaments**, some as long as thirty meters. They are fine, sticky, and nearly invisible, swaying beneath the creature like the tendrils of a vast airborne jellyfish.

At the front of the canopy sits a small, dense **sensory knot**, the closest thing the Drifter has to a head. It has no eyes in the traditional sense. Instead, it has a cluster of pit organs that detect heat and air pressure, plus a ring of light-sensitive patches that can read the flicker of other Drifters' lanterns.

## How It Flies

The Drifter is mostly a passive flier, a living kite. Its hollow ribs are filled with **hydrogen**, produced by symbiotic bacteria that break down the sugars the Drifter photosynthesizes through its canopy. By releasing or storing gas through tiny valves, it can rise and sink with surprising precision.

To steer, it ripples the edges of its canopy in slow waves, much as a cuttlefish moves its fins. Most of the time, though, it simply rides the endless winds of the Twilight Band, circling the planet in great migratory loops that take about forty Earth days to complete.

The Drifter feeds in two ways:

## Its World

The Duskwader lives on **Thessaly**, a rocky planet tidally locked to a dim red dwarf star. One hemisphere faces its sun forever and bakes; the other lies in endless frozen night. Between them runs the **terminator**, a ring of permanent twilight where the sun hangs motionless on the horizon like a swollen ember. Because hot air rises on the dayside and rushes toward the cold nightside, the terminator is scoured by a wind that never stops and always blows in the same direction.

The Duskwader has evolved to live entirely within this wind.

## Appearance

A grown Duskwader stands about six meters tall on **three long, jointed legs** arranged in a tripod, the most stable stance against a gale that has never once let up in its species' history. The legs are hollow, segmented like bamboo, and pale gray, with tiny valves along their length.

Atop the legs sits a narrow, keel-shaped body, streamlined like the hull of a boat. From its back rises its most striking feature: a **vast membranous sail**, ribbed with flexible spines and colored a deep violet-black. On a world lit only by weak red light, black is the most efficient color for absorbing energy, so the sail looks less like a fin than like a scrap of night sky stretched over bone.

It has no distinct head. Along the front edge of its body runs a row of **feathery combs**, and beneath them a cluster of glossy, heat-sensing pits that glow faintly when the animal is alert.

## How It Feeds

The Duskwader eats in two ways.

1. **Light-drinking:** Its sail is packed with symbiotic microbes that photosynthesize the dim red sunlight and share sugars with their host. When fully unfurled, the sail can stretch twenty meters across.
2. **Wind-combing:** The endless wind carries clouds of spores, pollen-like particles, and tiny drifting organisms from the fertile dayside. The Duskwader faces the wind and lets its combs filter this "aerial plankton," like a whale sifting krill.

## The Long Tack

The two methods of feeding pull against each other, and this tension shapes the animal's whole life.

With its sail raised, the Duskwader catches the wind and is slowly pushed **nightward**, into colder, darker country where the light fades but the wind-blown food grows richer. When light grows too scarce, it folds its sail flat and begins the slow walk **back toward the sun**, leaning into the gale on its three legs.

Herds of Duskwaders spend their entire lives in this rhythm, drifting into darkness and trudging back to dusk, a cycle observers might call "the long tack." From a distance a herd looks like a fleet of dark ships tilting across a red-lit plain.

## Senses and Song

In a world of constant wind and dim light, the Duskwader relies on:

- **Infrared pits** that let it "see" warm bodies and terrain in the gloom.
- **Fine hairs** along its legs that read shifts in wind speed and direction, warning of storms.
- **Vibration sense** through its feet, picking up footsteps and distant rockfalls through the ground.

Its hollow legs also give it a voice. By opening and closing the valves along them, a Duskwader turns the wind into **long, organ-like tones**. Each individual has a signature chord, and herds harmonize to stay together in dust storms. On calm stretches of the terminator, the low droning of a herd can carry for kilometers.

## Danger From Above and Below

Red dwarf stars are prone to violent **flares** that bathe the surface in radiation. When the Duskwader's pits detect the sudden flash, it collapses its sail, folds its legs, and crouches low. Its skin shifts within seconds to a **silvery, reflective sheen**, and the herd presses together until the flare passes.

Its main predator is the **tetherer**, a flat, burrowing ambusher that lies buried in the dust and fires sticky filaments into the wind, hoping to snag a passing Duskwader's legs. Herds walk in staggered lines so that a snagged individual can be braced by its neighbors while it tears free.

## Life Cycle

Duskwaders reproduce by releasing hundreds of light, winged **seed-young** into the wind. These drift all the way to the frozen edge of the nightside, where most perish. The survivors lodge in ice hollows and feed on the deep drifts of frozen spores that have accumulated there for millennia.

Over several years they grow, sprout their legs, and finally begin a **lifelong walk sunward** to join the herds in the twilight. Every adult Duskwader has made this pilgrimage out of the dark.

## Death

When a Duskwader grows old, it locks its legs and simply stops, often facing the sun. Its body remains upright for decades, the hollow legs still whistling faintly in the wind. Small creatures nest in its ribs, and lichen-like growths colonize its sail. Old migration routes across Thessaly are marked by these standing skeletons, singing quietly in the endless gale.
